Yesterday we learned that a judge has allowed a $32 billion lawsuit to proceed, alleging that the facial recognition feature in Apple Photos violates state privacy laws.

This has been conflated with Meta's use of facial recognition, even though the two companies' practices are at opposite ends of the privacy spectrum. The court's decision to allow this case to proceed shows a fundamental misunderstanding of how this feature works…

The Earlier Lawsuit Against Meta

To properly understand this, we need to start with a lawsuit against Meta over facial recognition, dating back to 2015.

Because that facial recognition process happened on Meta's servers, and Meta could identify those faces, the company was indeed in violation of the law and was ultimately forced to settle for $650 million.

Apple is now being sued under the same Illinois state law—the Biometric Information Privacy Act (BIPA)—which states that companies cannot collect biometric data without the subject's consent.

Apple's Approach Is Fundamentally Different

There's just one big problem with this allegation: when Apple performs facial recognition in the Apple Photos app, it absolutely does not collect any biometric data. As Apple pointed out in a machine learning research paper published in 2021, the recognition algorithm runs entirely on-device.

Beyond that, all the iPhone does is say "these photos all appear to be of the same person"—it has absolutely no idea who that person is. Only the iPhone user themselves can assign names to those faces.

Apple has also reiterated this in its Photos-related privacy policy.

I find it hard to believe that this lawsuit has been allowed to drag on through the legal system for six years now, but a few minutes of research makes it clear the allegations are obviously wrong.

The courts and legislators should be actively praising Apple's approach to privacy protection, not conflating it with privacy-destroying practices by companies like Meta.

This is yet another example of courts and legislators fundamentally not understanding the technology they are trying to regulate. The most obvious example is of course end-to-end encryption. Many countries have threatened or attempted to ban end-to-end encryption, despite clearly having no understanding of how the technology actually works.

Of course, I understand that judges and politicians cannot be experts in every area they need to deal with. But they do have access to experts, and what I find puzzling is that these lawsuits and legislative attempts can run for so many years in the legal system without anyone pointing out such a basic error.
